transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-03-11 14:30 UTC | Duration: ~42m | Recording: yes
Attendees: Alex Mercer (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (CS brief), Marta Ruiz (Polaris Head of Platform), Lee Chen (Backend), Samir Patel (Security), Ava Gomez (Product)

[00:00] Alex: hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh I'm Alex from Redwood Inference. Quick agenda — we'll do a 20-minute walkthrough of hosted chat (streaming + params), then a console demo showing routing/fallbacks, and end with Q&A and next steps. Priya's on to show the latency bits.

[00:23] Marta: thanks Alex, appreciate it. We're mainly focused on real-time triage for patient-chat flows. Low latency matters and of course data residency / encryption.

[00:35] Alex: got it. Totally - low latency and encryption are common. Priya, do you want to start on streaming?

[00:42] Priya: yeah sure. So the hosted chat endpoint streams tokens as they're generated. You get partial chunks — depending on your client you can pipe them into the UI. The tip is to tune chunk sizes and the flush interval on the client side to match your UX needs.

[01:12] Lee: when you say chunk sizes, is that per token or per N tokens? How do we control that?

[01:20] Priya: good question. The runtime streams as tokens are emitted by the model, but the HTTP layer may coalesce bytes for efficiency. On the Console you can enable smaller stream frames or keep default batching — smaller frames reduce latency but increase per-request overhead. We also have a streaming param — stream_delta_ms in the SDK — but most customers stick to defaults.

[02:03] Marta: for us, average prompt seq len is 600, sometimes up to 1k. We're worried about latency at p95.

[02:15] Priya: noted. For 600-1k it's helpful to pin a model variant optimized for long context. On hosted we surface perf profiles in the model catalog; pick one with verified p95 numbers at that seq len. Also enable KV cache for chat histories to avoid re-encoding long prefixes.

[03:01] Samir: quick sec — security. How is data at rest encrypted? Can you bring our KMS? We also need SSO, audit logs, and a retention policy.

[03:12] Alex: yes — hosted supports customer-managed KMS via our Enterprise plan, and we emit audit logs, plus SAML SSO and RBAC controls. For retention we have per-tenant configs; we can redact or store for x days. We'll send the SOC 2 + network diagram after this call.

[03:48] Marta: please, that'll be helpful.

[04:00] Priya: back to streaming — retries are important. We recommend idempotency keys for user requests. If you retry, attach the same idempotency key so the runtime can dedupe and avoid duplicate token billing. For streaming specifically, client libraries help with reconnection — we do an offset-based resume for short disconnects.

[04:42] Lee: offset resume? how reliable is that across network blips?

[04:51] Priya: it's robust for transient TCP resets, up to a few seconds. For longer disconnects the safe pattern is to re-request with the idempotency key and let the server return the final generation, or fallback to a shorter context.

[05:30] Alex: another lever is our automatic fallback routing: if the primary model is throttled we can route to a cheaper, quantized variant — with config to preserve safety checks. That reduces 503s for your users.

[05:52] Ava: so that means possible slight quality drop but better availability?

[05:57] Alex: exactly. You can set a policy: prefer the high-quality model until queue latency crosses threshold, then fallback to the cheaper variant. Console shows that routing and you can preview sample outputs.

[06:30] Priya: I'll show the console in a sec. Quick note on params: temperature controls randomness, top_p too if you use nucleus sampling, and max_tokens is enforced at the server side. Cost is per-token generated + per-input token. We also surface token breakdown in the Console.

[07:05] Lee: do you support streaming function call semantics? We do toolcalling for some structured outputs.

[07:12] Priya: yes, function/tool calling is supported — the streaming includes function call tokens and then a final tool payload. The SDK exposes partial function tokens so you can start parsing before finalization. Slight caveat: if you use function calling + streaming and a reconnect happens, use idempotency keys to ensure function side effects are not duplicated.

[08:00] Marta: about throughput — our traffic is spiky, mostly morning rush with bursts. Can Redwood autoscale?

[08:12] Alex: hosted autoscaling handles sudden spikes; for guaranteed capacity we recommend Dedicated. But hosted has burst capacity and smart routing across regions. For very predictable SLA you can choose Reserved capacity.

[08:45] Samir: what about data residency? We need EU-only.

[08:52] Alex: hosted has region controls; we can pin traffic to eu-west, and for stricter needs there's Private (VPC) deployment where the control plane is separated. We'll include docs comparing Hosted vs Private for compliance needs.

[09:20] Priya: jumping into the Console now — sharing my screen (note: occasional webcam frozen, audio hiccup, small crosstalk). On the model catalog page you can filter models by token cost, p95 latency at seq len. Here's an example of a quantized small model and a higher-quality float16 variant.

[10:05] [screen share] Priya: you can set per-route policies — e.g., route production chat to model-A with fallback to model-B, add an automatic rollback window if quality regressions are detected. The Optimize tab suggests batching configs and cache TTLs based on your traffic pattern.

[11:00] Lee: about batching — our backend aggregates multiple user queries where possible. Will batching harm latency?

[11:10] Priya: batching reduces per-token cost but can add a small waiting latency while the batch fills. For low-latency paths we recommend small batch sizes and dynamic batching thresholds (time-based). Optimize analyzes your request histogram and recommends a sweet spot.

[12:02] Ava: do you expose token-level costs in the API response?

[12:08] Priya: not per request in the payload, but Console and billing APIs provide token breakdown per call id. We can also enable lightweight headers with a token estimate to log on your side.

[12:40] Alex: ok demo moment — we'll trigger a streaming example. Priya, start the example with a multi-turn chat.

[12:50] Priya: starting now — sending a prompt: "Patient: I have a sore throat and fever; what should I do?" Streaming partials incoming... [12:58] partial: "Hi — I'm not a doctor but if you're experiencing fever..." [13:22] final: "Advise rest, hydrate, monitor temp; seek care if high fever or breathing issues". 

[13:40] Lee: latency saw ~180ms for initial chunk, whole response 750ms. That's good. How do you measure those numbers?

[13:52] Priya: Console shows server-side first-byte and end timings. For client-to-server RTT we recommend instrumenting on the client. Also note that seq len and model variant heavily impact those numbers.

[14:30] Marta: in production we log everything to our ELK. Can we push request traces and model ids?

[14:38] Alex: yep, we can push request-level traces to a webhook or integrate with your tracing system. We'll show an example payload after the call.

[15:05] Samir: two security deep items — do you support HSM for KMS? And can we rotate keys without downtime?

[15:16] Alex: we integrate with customer KMS/HSM providers and support key rotation. Rotation is non-disruptive; we maintain a key ring and gracefully roll. We'll pass the technical note.

[15:45] Priya: quick note on retries — we recommend a client-side linear/backoff with jitter for status codes 429/503. For idempotent generation requests, use idempotency keys; for streaming, reconnect and attempt resume.

[16:10] Lee: any guidance for retry counts? We're worried about compounding load.

[16:18] Priya: common pattern: try 1 immediate retry with the same idempotency key, then exponential backoff x2 up to 3 attempts. For large traffic consider circuit-breaker at the app layer. The Console has a per-route rate-limiter and quota you can tune.

[17:00] Ava: about function calling reliability — if the tool is triggered twice due to a retry, how do we prevent duplicate side effects?

[17:10] Priya: that's an app-level concern — use idempotency keys/session ids for your tool endpoints. On our side we provide the original request id in the function call payload header so your service can dedupe.

[17:42] Alex: back to cost — Optimize will recommend quantization or smaller model variants for high-volume background tasks, while keeping high-quality float models for user-facing chat. That hybrid approach cuts costs.

[18:10] Marta: can we do a short pilot just on our triage chat to validate latency and cost?

[18:20] Alex: yes — pilot is perfect. We'll propose a 3-month pilot scope: 100k/ month tokens, p95 < 800ms for your 600-1k seq len, and failover policy configured.

[18:42] Priya: Priya to run the latency test with their sample prompts after Marta shares the prompt set. We'll produce a CSV with p50/p95/p99 numbers and model variant used.

[19:05] Lee: one thing — when fallback occurs, can we run an A/B test to compare outputs? We'd like to know quality delta.

[19:12] Priya: yes, Console supports canary/A-B rollouts and stores evals. You can wire in your eval set and we'll produce difference metrics (BLEU-ish and hallucination counts if you provide anchors).

[19:50] Marta: excellent. A couple of obscure questions — does your runtime support multi-GPU sharded serving for very long-context models?

[20:02] Priya: we do multi-GPU shards for certain families; for hosted it's transparent. For Dedicated/Private you can choose sharded allocation depending on model size and we handle KV cache across shards. There's a slight increase in cross-GPU latency but it's optimized.

[20:40] Samir: about logs/audit: can we query per-user tokens and redact PHI? We need to ensure PHI never lands in logs.

[20:52] Alex: we can configure redaction, and for PHI-sensitive flows we typically recommend Private deployment + no logging or on-prem ingestion with private control plane. We'll include the options.

[21:20] Ava: technical nit — you mentioned stream_delta_ms. Is that exposed in the REST API or only SDK?

[21:27] Priya: SDK exposes it; REST can pass a header param but it's easier via SDK. The header is x-redwood-stream-ms. We also have client libs that manage reconnection logic.

[22:05] [brief silence while Priya navigates Console]

[22:28] Priya: showing Optimize tab — here it recommends batching=4 for background summarization and batch=1 for low-latency chat. Also suggests cache TTL of 30 minutes for repeated context prompts.

[23:00] Lee: that's helpful. How do you surface regressions?

[23:07] Priya: we track prompt-based evals and run continuous comparisons across model versions; if quality drops outside a threshold the rollout is automatically halted and rolled back, and alerts ping the console and email.

[23:38] Marta: can we white-label any of the telemetry? We prefer not to expose internal IDs to end users.

[23:45] Alex: yes telemetry can be scrubbed and you control what surfaces to end users. We send minimal headers for privacy.

[24:10] Samir: we're close on security but need to see SOC2 and the network diagram and confirm SAML integration.

[24:20] Alex: will do. I'll attach those docs and the link to our compliance page in the follow-up.

[24:40] Priya: quick live test for a reconnect scenario: I simulate a 3s TCP reset then attempt resume with same idempotency key — resume succeeds and server returns the rest of the tokens. Note: if the disconnect was longer we fall back to re-request mode.

[25:12] Lee: good to know. What logging do you keep for idempotent operations?

[25:20] Priya: request id, idempotency key, model variant, timestamps; we keep those in audit logs but can redact payloads.

[26:00] Alex: ok, wrap-up — agreed next steps: Alex to send SOC2 + network diagram; Priya to run bench after Marta shares prompt set; Alex to share pilot pricing. Proposed pilot kickoff Mar 18.

[26:25] Marta: sounds good. Can you also include sample eval reports?

[26:32] Priya: yes, we'll include a sample eval PDF.

[27:00] Ava: timeline-wise — procurement/PO will need lead time; what's typical for enterprise onboarding?

[27:10] Alex: 2-4 weeks for basic contracts and security review, longer if on-prem. Since you prefer hosted in EU it should be on the faster side.

[27:40] Samir: will we get a staging VPC for testing?

[27:48] Alex: yes, we'll provide a sandbox tenant in eu-west for testing during the pilot.

[28:10] [short Q&A about billing meters]

[29:00] Lee: final quick: do you have a sample SDK for Android (mobile)? We plan to integrate a lightweight client.

[29:12] Priya: we have JS, Python, Go SDKs. For mobile we provide a thin REST helper plus examples for Android/ios to stream and reconnect. We'll drop sample snippets.

[30:00] Marta: ok thanks everyone.

[30:05] Alex: final notes — I'll send the follow-up with links. One more question from Jordan: any recommended start params for safety filtering?

[30:20] Jordan (CS): they want default safety filters and moderation hooks.

[30:25] Priya: we expose a safety middleware — apply the safety channel on the model route; Console can auto-run moderation checks. For PHI flows you might want deterministic safety with stronger filters—we can show configs.

[31:00] Ava: great. Let's reconvene after you share docs and Priya's bench.

[31:10] Alex: thanks all. We'll follow-up with SOC2, pricing, sandbox details, and the bench results. Any final items?

[31:30] Marta: none from me. Thanks.

[31:35] Samir: thanks, bye.

[31:37] Meeting end (note: recording continues for a few seconds)

Notes: occasional transcription glitches — e.g., "K V cash" heard instead of KV cache in a couple places; speaker labels had small mismatches at join/leave.

References shared: Console demo link (ephemeral): https://console.redwood.ai/demo/session/3489 (link to be shared in follow-up), SOC2 & security pack: https://redwood.ai/security/soc2 (to be attached).
